paragraphs: Friend, this passage shows two men in the same chapter with a lot of power or a lot of people around them, and they do opposite things with it. Saul sits under a tree with his spear in hand and all his servants around him, and he is so afraid of losing his grip that he sees plots everywhere. David is hiding in a cave, and he ends up with about four hundred men who were distressed, in debt or discontented (1 Samuel 22:1-2, 6). Here's the lesson: fear makes a person grab and swing, and care makes a person open the door.

Saul's fear gets worse and worse until he orders the killing of the priests of the LORD, and his own servants "would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD" (1 Samuel 22:17). Ahimelech spoke up for David and said he knew nothing of the affair, and it didn't change the king's mind (1 Samuel 22:14-16). I think this is one of the heaviest passages in the whole story, and it's okay to sit quietly with that. It also teaches that a heart full of fear and anger can do terrible harm, and the people who pay for it are often the ones who did nothing to deserve it.

Then Abiathar, the one son who got away, runs to David, and look at what David says: "Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me." (1 Samuel 22:23). David owns his part too, saying, "I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father's house" (1 Samuel 22:22). So this is for you, baker: be the kind of person who makes room for the hurting and owns your part, because that beats being the one who clutches the spear. And the story isn't over, friend. We're only at passage 8 of 17.
